motion: Does the God of the Bible exist?

bridges.description: Establish that the specifically biblical God exists.
Argue that the biblical God is necessary for knowledge, logic, and intelligible experience.
Connect the proposed foundation to the triune God revealed in scripture.
Defend biblical descriptions through contextual and worldview-sensitive interpretation.
Ground moral judgment in God and defend divine judgment against harm-based objections.
Deny the existence of the specifically described God of the Bible.
Argue that incompatible biblical descriptions and deeds make the depicted being impossible.
Use allegedly failed prayer promises and absent miracles against the depicted God.
Challenge the inference from philosophical foundations to the biblical God and scripture.
Use harm minimization to criticize biblical commands and actions.

sections.title: Motion Scope and Burdens
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute what each side must establish and whether general worldview claims reach the specific biblical God.

sections.title: Logic and Intelligibility
sections.rationale: Ayala's main constructive case and Barker's alternative account concern whether knowledge and logic require the biblical God.

sections.title: Trinitarian Grounding and Rival Worldviews
sections.rationale: Ayala's one-and-many argument and the later Hindu comparison test whether the proposed foundation uniquely selects biblical Trinitarianism.

sections.title: Revelation and Biblical Identity
sections.rationale: The bridge from philosophical foundations to the particular scriptures and triune God is repeatedly tested.

sections.title: Prayer and Scriptural Coherence
sections.rationale: Prayer promises, qualifications, and alleged contradictions form a distinct evidential exchange.

sections.title: Competing Moral Standards
sections.rationale: The speakers develop rival accounts of what authorizes moral criticism.

sections.title: Suffering and Divine Judgment
sections.rationale: Concrete suffering and biblical punishments test whether the depicted God's conduct coheres with claimed goodness and justice.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: The biblical God exists necessarily rather than merely probably.
moves.warrant: The biblical God's revealed attributes provide the necessary preconditions for intelligibility and knowledge.
moves.inference: If those preconditions require this God, the contrary is impossible and the motion is affirmed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This opening passage states Ayala's exact modal thesis and its intelligibility warrant.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it is impossible for God not to exist
necessary preconditions for intelligibility and by extension knowledge itself
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the opening to Ayala, who announces his proposition and case.
moves.importanceRationale: This states Ayala's adopted motion-level thesis.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly affirms the motion through a necessity claim.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: If knowledge and intelligible experience are possible, the Christian worldview is true.
moves.warrant: Knowledge and intelligible experience are possible.
moves.inference: Therefore the Christian worldview is true and the God of the Bible exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the named argument, both premises, and the stated conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if knowledge and intelligible experience are even possible
Therefore, the Christian worldview is true
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ayala opening with an explicitly enumerated argument.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the formal core of Ayala's main constructive case.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes intelligibility the route to the Christian conclusion.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: The Christian God grounds truth, logic, reliable cognition, moral reasoning, and nature's regularity.
moves.warrant: God is presented as ultimate, personal, rational, righteous, creator of human knowers, and providential governor of nature.
moves.inference: Those attributes supply the preconditions Ayala says knowledge and science require.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala makes one compound grounding argument: the span first enumerates five claimed preconditions, then matches each to a divine attribute. Shortening it would silently omit one of the speaker's stated premise-to-ground links.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the laws of logic, which must be
regularity upon which science and induction depend
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous constructive explanation in Ayala's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It warrants the first premise of the transcendental syllogism.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how the proposed God supplies each alleged precondition.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: The Trinity provides a foundation for unity and diversity as equally ultimate.
moves.warrant: God is one being in three persons, so neither unity nor plurality is derivative in the divine nature.
moves.inference: Abstract universals and particular facts can both be grounded in the triune God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Ayala's complete one-and-many argument, from the stated philosophical problem through the Trinitarian grounding conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God is one in being, three in persons
Unity and diversity are equally ultimate in his nature
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ayala opening statement with no speaker change.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ayala's specific Trinitarian uniqueness bridge rather than a generic restatement of intelligibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects the preconditions argument to the distinctively Trinitarian biblical God.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The biblical God does not exist because promised prayer outcomes and miracles do not occur.
moves.warrant: Barker cites biblical promises of healing and answered prayer, then contrasts them with a child's death and ordinary success rates.
moves.inference: A truthful miracle-working God who makes those promises would produce observable fulfillment, so their failure counts against that being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the parents' reliance on biblical healing promises, includes the quoted promise sequence, and ends with Barker's explicit nonexistence inference; earlier biographical detail and later analogies are not needed.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: prayers are not answered. Therefore, the God of the Bible does not exist
every time you pray a petitionary or intercessory prayer
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator introduces Barker's opening, which continues uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: Barker calls this his main argument and returns to it later.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents failed promises as evidence against the biblical God's existence.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The biblical God's stated attributes conflict with attributed deeds and descriptions.
moves.warrant: Barker contrasts goodness, justice, mercy, constancy, power, and knowledge with a catalog of contrary biblical depictions.
moves.inference: A being defined by mutually incompatible characteristics cannot exist as described.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This continuous catalog supports Barker's explicit incompatibility principle before he changes topics.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: A being with mutually incompatible characteristics cannot exist
He says he is merciful then commits merciless acts
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening with no speaker handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Barker's other central route to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It alleges contradictions within the biblical God's defining description.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A divine revelation requiring disputed expert explanations reflects an inept communicator.
moves.warrant: The intended reader cannot reliably grasp the Bible's true meaning without sectarian interpreters.
moves.inference: Interpretive dependence undermines the claim that the Bible is a perfect revelation from an intelligent and benevolent God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the communication argument after a logistical water request and before the next argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: why should the perfect word of a loving God have to be explained
God is inept. He's a bad communicator
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening; the preceding water request is excluded.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the public revelation link rather than one isolated verse.

burdenContact.rationale: It attacks scripture's capacity to identify and communicate the relevant God.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Suffering does not logically entail that the biblical God does not exist.
moves.warrant: The Christian worldview can attribute suffering to a fallen world and morally sufficient divine purposes.
moves.inference: Even an emotionally forceful case does not establish contradiction or nonexistence without defeating that possible explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's passage reconstructs the inference, supplies his fallen-world answer, and states the logical consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it still doesn't logically follow that God doesn't exist
we live in a fallen world
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala speaks continuously in his named rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his direct response to Barker's opening suffering case.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a reconciliation meant to block Barker's contradiction inference.

responseComponents.description: Denies that the child's suffering by itself entails nonexistence.
Offers a fallen-world and divine-purpose reconciliation.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Confusion about scripture may arise from readers rather than from God or the Bible.
moves.warrant: People can lack education or interpretive effort, while difficult passages remain compatible with sufficient overall clarity.
moves.inference: Disagreement and individual ignorance do not entail that the biblical God does not exist.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage states the reader-fault alternative, qualification about difficulty, and nonexistence consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Why can't it be the fault of individuals
my ignorance doesn't entail the God of the Bible
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ayala rebuttal addressing Barker's clarity argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Barker's public-communication objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends scripture as sufficiently clear despite interpretive difficulty.

responseComponents.description: Offers reader limitations as an alternative source of confusion.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: General philosophical foundations do not by themselves establish the God of the Bible.
moves.warrant: Other theistic positions could accept similar philosophical arguments while rejecting the biblical character.
moves.inference: Ayala must bridge transcendental reasoning to the specifically biblical God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's focused rebuttal runs from debate scope through the explicit bridge question.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how do you get from there to the God of the Bible
I don't have to be an atheist up here
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator introduces Barker's rebuttal, and he speaks continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It tests whether Ayala's main argument reaches the exact motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It demands the missing particularizing inference.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether the necessity claim identifies the biblical God.
Challenges the move from intelligibility to Christianity.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Morality can be evaluated by whether conduct minimizes or maximizes harm.
moves.warrant: Physical and psychological harms are natural effects that can be compared and measured.
moves.inference: Biblical acts creating unnecessary harm can be judged immoral without a cosmic moral object.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage introduces Barker's metric, explains its natural basis, and applies it to the biblical God.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: If you're acting with the intention of minimizing harm
the God of the Bible is immoral
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal after his scope argument.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Barker's recurring standard for moral objections.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the evaluative rule used by the con case.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Specific biblical punishments conflict with the claim that the biblical God is just.
moves.warrant: Barker cites punishment of David through his wives and inherited exclusions from worship.
moves.inference: A being who claims justice but performs unjust acts is internally inconsistent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains the examples and Barker's cancellation inference before he changes topics.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: should my wife be raped for it
if he says one thing and he does another
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal; the questions are clearly his challenges.
moves.importanceRationale: It gives concrete support for Barker's moral incoherence strand.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies the contradiction claim to justice.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Christian claims about God's nature are derived from scripture.
moves.warrant: Ayala gives God's spirituality and other attributes as examples of beliefs obtained from biblical texts.
moves.inference: Barker's concession that Christianity can be internally consistent bears on the God described by scripture.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This mixed span starts with Ayala's renewed question and ends with his quoted consistency evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: where do you think our theology comes from
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala's questions and examples carry the claim; Barker's interjection is target context only.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses the identity bridge between philosophy and the biblical character.

burdenContact.rationale: It locates the attributed divine nature in scripture.

responseComponents.description: Answers the demand for a biblical connection by locating attributes in scripture.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Barker's lack-of-belief definition conflicts with the biblical claim that everyone knows God.
moves.warrant: Romans 1, as Ayala presents it, says all people possess sufficient knowledge of God and are without excuse.
moves.inference: Barker's self-description implicitly denies a biblical proposition and is a worldview commitment rather than neutrality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's cross-examination sequence states Barker's definition, the Romans 1 premise, and the clarified worldview inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all men have a knowledge of God
That is a worldview position
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala explicitly frames and repeats the question; Barker's request for clarification is not evidence for Ayala's claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the actual burden argument to which Barker's lack-belief distinction responds.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that Barker's stated stance denies a biblical claim and is not neutral.

responseComponents.description: Challenges Barker's attempt to bracket his broader stance from the motion.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Lacking belief in a god differs from affirmatively believing no god exists.
moves.warrant: An atheist can withhold belief while allowing that a god might exist.
moves.inference: Barker's general atheism does not automatically assume every positive burden Ayala assigns to it.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's compact answer states the distinction and modal consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a lack of belief is not the same as a belief in a lack
Maybe he exists. Maybe he could exist
moves.attributionRationale: Barker answers Ayala directly in an uninterrupted turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It clarifies the burden Barker accepts outside his specific arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It limits the con burden to the case Barker actually advances.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes withholding belief from the positive denial Ayala says Romans 1 entails.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Barker cannot use logic against Christianity without relying on the foundation Ayala attributes to the Christian God.
moves.warrant: Universal immaterial laws need a metaphysical ground supplied by the biblical God's attributes.
moves.inference: Barker's logical objections allegedly presuppose and thereby confirm Ayala's foundation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's answer gives the grounding claim, borrowing challenge, and intended consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how do you use logic to object to my position
You're proving him in forming your objections
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala speaks continuously in his own cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: Ayala treats this recurring reply as his strongest proof.

burdenContact.rationale: It turns Barker's use of logic into support for the alleged foundation.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the availability of Barker's logical standard.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Ayala has not shown that the biblical God is the source of logic.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes Ayala's modern Christian philosophical account from a demonstration grounded in scripture.
moves.inference: Using logic in an objection does not by itself establish the specifically biblical source Ayala claims.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's direct response isolates the missing biblical bridge after Ayala's borrowing challenge and stops before Ayala answers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you have not shown that the God of the Bible is the source of logic
you have not shown it from scripture
moves.attributionRationale: Barker directly answers Ayala's immediately preceding borrowing challenge; the opening overlap carries Ayala's final phrase before Barker's objection.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the specific source claim needed to connect the transcendental argument to the debate's biblical motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the proposed grounding has not been tied to the biblical text.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference from Barker's use of logic to the biblical God as logic's demonstrated source.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Logic is a useful formalized activity of minds rather than an independently existing cosmic object.
moves.warrant: Its exercise requires functioning intelligence and can be regular across human cognition.
moves.inference: Logic need not have the transcendent personal source Ayala proposes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage captures Barker's positive account and his exercise-versus-object qualification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Logic is a useful tool that humans are using
moves.attributionRationale: Formal cross-examination makes turn ownership clear; Barker's answers supply the claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Barker's direct alternative account of the disputed precondition.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies that using logic uniquely identifies a divine source.

responseComponents.description: Offers a non-divine account of logical practice.
Denies that using logic borrows Christian metaphysics.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: If the biblical God has the attributed omniscience and righteousness, he knows the full context in which judgments are just.
moves.warrant: Barker accepts conditionally that such a God would know the relevant context, while Ayala argues that scripture supplies those attributes.
moves.inference: Barker's examples do not establish internal inconsistency merely by appearing unjust from limited human context.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala restates Barker's context-dependent moral premise, asks whether the omniscient biblical God would know the proper context for judgment, receives Barker's conditional concession, and draws the non-inconsistency inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: he would know the proper context
So, by definition, so then it's not inconsistent
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala's words frame the claimed defense; Barker's brief questions and conditional answer are target context and are not attributed to Ayala.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a substantive direct defense of divine acts distinct from challenging Barker's moral standard.

burdenContact.rationale: It uses divine knowledge and character to answer alleged unjust acts.

responseComponents.description: Answers the injustice examples by appealing to the full context known by an omniscient and righteous God.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Ayala must explain how he knows human-authored biblical texts are revelation from beyond the universe.
moves.warrant: The words appear on pages written by human beings, so their claimed origin beyond the universe still requires support.
moves.inference: Philosophical or internal coherence by itself does not establish that these writings are divine revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's opening cross-examination question isolates the epistemic issue before Ayala answers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how do you know that those words written on those pages
actually revelation from some ghost from outside the universe
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the cross-examination to Barker, who addresses Ayala's revelation claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the route from philosophy to scripture.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks what makes this text specifically revelatory.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the basis for treating scripture as divine.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Ayala knows scripture through the Spirit's internal witness while publicly justifying that trust through his transcendental argument.
moves.warrant: Believers recognize God's voice in scripture, while the opening argument is offered as a distinct justification.
moves.inference: Private recognition and debate-facing justification operate through related but distinguishable routes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's full answer preserves both the internal-witness claim and his distinction from public justification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: his spirit has bore witness to my spirit
that's different than how we justify it
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala answers continuously and corrects Barker's one-part summary.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ayala's fullest account of how revelation is known and defended.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies recognition and a public argumentative route to scripture.

responseComponents.description: Separates internal knowledge from public justification.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Appealing to God's authority to authenticate God's revelation appears circular.
moves.warrant: The claimed revelation identifies the authority, while the authority is used to validate the revelation.
moves.inference: Ayala has not supplied an independent discriminator for this scripture over competing revelation claims.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The exchange contains Ayala's authority claim and Barker's focused circularity question, stopping before Ayala's answer.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: isn't that circular
moves.attributionRationale: Barker's question is clear; Ayala's answer is included only as target context.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the epistemic structure of the particular revelation claim.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the proposed biblical identifier lacks independent support.

responseComponents.description: Tests whether the stated knowledge and justification routes escape circular authentication.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Circularity at an ultimate foundation is unavoidable and not automatically fallacious.
moves.warrant: Reasoning and sensory reliability must themselves be used when anyone attempts to justify reasoning or sensory reliability.
moves.inference: The comparison is which worldview can justify unavoidable foundational commitments, not whether it has no circularity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's uninterrupted answer states the ultimate-foundation principle, two examples, and the comparative conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: ultimate foundations are circular
my worldview can actually provide a rational justification
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala explicitly answers Barker's circularity question.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ayala's direct defense of his revelatory epistemology.

burdenContact.rationale: It reframes authentication as comparative worldview justification.

responseComponents.description: Argues that foundational circularity is universal and must be compared.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A competing claimed revelation about a deity above Yahweh tests whether Ayala has a general acceptance rule.
moves.warrant: Barker's hypothetical mirrors the form of an internal revelatory claim while contradicting the biblical hierarchy.
moves.inference: Rejecting the rival because it conflicts with prior Christian commitments would not independently verify Christianity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker introduces the explicitly hypothetical revelation and asks whether Ayala would accept it, stopping before the answer.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a beautiful white cat came up to me
Would you accept my revelation
moves.attributionRationale: Barker labels the scenario hypothetical; it is not treated as his adopted worldview.
moves.importanceRationale: It stress-tests Ayala's method for distinguishing revelation claims.

burdenContact.rationale: It probes whether scripture is selected by a generalizable criterion.

responseComponents.description: Tests the internal-witness route with a rival claim.
Tests whether comparative worldview evaluation is symmetric.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: A rival revelation must be tested within its worldview for whether it supplies coherent knowledge.
moves.warrant: If its deity produces or permits a lying subordinate revelation, the claimant loses a dependable epistemic basis.
moves.inference: Barker's hypothetical does not rival Christianity merely by matching the surface form of revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala identifies the lying-deity implication and states the resulting epistemic failure.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you've now you've now cut yourself off
how could you ever know anything about his revelation
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala develops the answer within Barker's explicitly hypothetical scenario.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies Ayala's substantive discriminator for the rival-revelation test.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies Ayala's coherence criterion to a competing revelation.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the rival on alleged epistemic consequences rather than mere difference.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: An alleged biblical contradiction fails if the passages have a possible reconciliation.
moves.warrant: A contradiction requires mutually exclusive propositions under the same conditions.
moves.inference: Apparently opposed wording does not establish contradiction when context permits another reading.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's answer states the interpretive premise and logical consequence before Barker changes topics.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if other interpretations are even possible
it logically follows that it's not a contradiction
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala responds directly during Barker-led cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ayala's general answer to Barker's contradiction catalog.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the reconciliation test used to defend scripture.

responseComponents.description: Argues that contextual reconciliation blocks incompatibility.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Reliance on multiple possible interpretations supports the charge that God communicated unclearly.
moves.warrant: Theologians, translators, and apologists dispute what the text means.
moves.inference: Interpretive escape routes may avoid formal contradiction while worsening the revelation's clarity problem.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker states the communication consequence and clarifies his face-value method before Ayala resumes.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: doesn't all of that basically prove my point that God was a bad communicator
we should start with the face value
moves.attributionRationale: Barker speaks in his own cross-examination; a humorous interruption does not alter the claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It converts Ayala's reconciliation defense into a revelation objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the defense carries a communication cost.

responseComponents.description: Argues that interpretive flexibility does not resolve communication.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Prayer promises must be read with the condition that requests accord with God's will.
moves.warrant: Ayala says Barker omitted the passage specifying that condition from his opening presentation.
moves.inference: The selected prayer texts do not constitute an unqualified universal promise and therefore do not form the alleged contradiction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's direct cross-examination answer identifies the omitted will-condition and states why its absence creates only an apparent contradiction.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if it is your will
cherrypicking verses to create contradictions
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala answers Barker's prayer question in a continuous turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the immediate answer targeted by Barker's next contradiction challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the specific qualification used to reconcile prayer passages.

responseComponents.description: Adds the will-condition Barker's opening prayer argument omitted.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: An unrestricted promise to answer prayer conflicts with a qualification that only requests fitting God's will are answered.
moves.warrant: Barker reads the unrestricted and qualified formulations as opposing claims.
moves.inference: The qualification does not rescue the promise but creates or reveals contradiction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's compact question states both formulations and the claimed contradiction.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I will answer all your prayers except for the ones
isn't that a contradiction
moves.attributionRationale: Barker asks the prayer question during his cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: It tests Barker's main prayer argument against Ayala's qualification.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues the qualification cannot reconcile the promise.

responseComponents.description: Argues that adding the will-condition conflicts with the apparently unrestricted promises.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Providing miracle studies would not resolve the dispute because evidence is interpreted through prior worldview commitments.
moves.warrant: Ayala predicts Barker would not accept such studies and says recognizing an act as miraculous requires a changed interpretive framework.
moves.inference: The absence of offered studies does not concede Barker's prayer argument, because Ayala locates the dispute at a prior worldview level.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's full audience reply moves from the request for miracle studies to his explicit reason for withholding specifics.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what would that prove
That you need a worldview to interpret whether something constitutes a miracle
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala continues his allotted answer; first-person reasons and references to Barker make ownership clear.
moves.importanceRationale: It explains why Ayala does not supply the empirical evidence Barker requests.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats miracle recognition as worldview-dependent rather than neutral disconfirmation.

responseComponents.description: Answers the demand for observable miracle confirmation by challenging its assumed interpretive neutrality.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Testable and repeatable evidence of biblical miracles would change Barker's mind.
moves.warrant: He says he seeks truth and would accept Christianity if prayer and miracle claims were solidly evidenced.
moves.inference: Ayala cannot dismiss the evidential request by attributing Barker's rejection to a closed or unchanged heart.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's uninterrupted response states openness, evidence conditions, and the answer to Ayala's motive attribution.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I would change my mind if I saw evidence of miracles
solid evidence that was testable, repeatable
moves.attributionRationale: Barker directly answers Ayala's immediately preceding claim about his likely reaction.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Barker's stated evidential posture and rebuts the reason for withholding evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It renews the request for observable support for miracle claims.

responseComponents.description: Directly denies Ayala's prediction that evidence could not change Barker's mind.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Moral action aims to minimize overall harm even when some immediate harm is necessary.
moves.warrant: Amputation illustrates that a local harm can prevent greater harm, while real policies can be compared by effects.
moves.inference: A natural harm standard can guide judgment without perfect knowledge or divine command.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Barker's full audience answer handles time horizon, necessary harm, measurement, and uncertainty.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: You might have to cause harm to minimize harm
the least amount of harm in it
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator directs the question to Barker, who answers continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It develops the con moral standard against a counterexample.

burdenContact.rationale: It refines how harms are compared over time.

moves.speaker: Eli Ayala
moves.claim: Defining morality as harm minimization does not explain why dissenters are objectively wrong.
moves.warrant: Agreement or restating Barker's preferred definition does not establish its truth or authority.
moves.inference: Without a normative foundation, the harm metric cannot bear Barker's judgment on God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Ayala's response states the dissent problem and counting-noses warrant through his conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: What happens when someone defines uh morality in a different way
You don't get truth by counting noses
moves.attributionRationale: Ayala receives the response turn and speaks continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ayala's central objection to Barker's standard.

burdenContact.rationale: It contests the authority of the standard used against God.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the original definition's authority.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Logic has three distinct pro moves—the formal syllogism, attribute-grounding warrant, and borrowing reply—against Barker's biblical-source challenge and positive mental-tool alternative. Trinitarian uniqueness retains Ayala's one-and-many construction, explicit biblical indications, and reply to Barker's single Hindu rival proposal. Moral standards retains Barker's initial harm definition, time-horizon refinement, and direct objectivity defense against Ayala's distinct normative-authority challenge. Each asymmetric move performs separate inferential work.
